..
Issued at 233 PM CDT Mon Sep 28 2026

Early afternoon analysis showed an upper level ridge axis 
passing through with low level clouds slowly but surely eroding 
from south to north. Temperatures as of 1 PM were in the mid 60s
to lower 70s.

The main focus in the forecast will be widespread rainfall 
expected Tuesday through Thursday. A strong upper level trough 
currently over the Desert Southwest remains on track to ingest 
tropical moisture from Hurricane Polo and edge eastward on 
Tuesday with a surface low spinning up ahead of the trough and 
eventually pushing northeast toward the area on Wednesday. In 
addition, we'll have a decent stream of moisture coming in from 
the gulf which, when combined with the tropical moisture from 
the southwest, will lead to precipitable water values exceeding 
2 inches per NAEFS and EPS guidance, exceeding the 
climatological maximum for this time of year. As warm air 
advection and moisture transport ramp up ahead of this system, 
showers and storms will develop to our west and push into 
northeast NE by early Tuesday morning. Precip will gradually 
overspread the area, lingering through Thursday before a cold 
front slides through and pushes the precip out.

With the aforementioned moisture availability/origin, moisture 
transport pointing into the area, and warm cloud depths 
exceeding 4 km, all the ingredients appear to be there for some 
very efficient rain producing showers and storms. Add in the 
fact that most of the area has received 2 to 5 inches of rain in
the last couple weeks leading to saturated soils and slightly 
elevated river levels, we're primed for flooding impacts. The 
big question is where the heaviest band of rain will fall. Model
consensus paints a broad band of 2-4" across much of the 
forecast area through Thursday with individual models 
highlighting potential for a narrow (~30 mile wide) band of 5-7
inches somewhere in there. Unfortunately, there remains quite a
bit of spread in that band, with solutions ranging from it 
falling across central into far northeast NE to north-central KS
into far southeast NE/far southwest IA. For what it's worth, 
highest probabilities for those 5+ inch amounts (20-30% chance) 
stretch from Butler County, east through the Omaha metro area 
and northeast into Harrison/Shelby Counties. Obviously, where 
that falls will significantly impact which rivers will see the 
highest potential for flooding, but at this point, at least the 
Missouri, Platte, Elkhorn, Big Blue, and Nishnabotna Rivers all 
have at least some potential for flooding. As such, a Flood 
Watch has been issued for much of the area from Tuesday evening 
through Thursday. Keep a close eye on the forecast, especially 
if you have interests near rivers.

If the flooding potential wasn't enough, there is at least some
small concern for severe thunderstorms, especially on Wednesday
as the surface low pushes closer to the area. While most 
guidance suggests we'll be cloudy and rainy much of that time, a
few "extended" CAMs (e.g. 28.12Z NAMNest) hint at a little 
instability building across far southeast NE with very curvy 
low-level hodographs immediately northeast of the low. If this 
pans out, would need to keep an eye on severe storms potential, 
particularly tornadoes. Very low confidence that this pans out, 
but worth monitoring with such a dynamic system on the way.

As mentioned above, a cold front will pass through sometime 
late Thursday and bring an end to the precip with surface high 
pressure building in. A few weak shortwave troughs look to pass 
by just to our north Friday and Saturday, but consensus 
generally keeps associated precip out of our area, giving us 
only a 5-10% chance High temperatures will be in the upper 60s 
to mid 70s through Wednesday, with lower to mid 60s through the 
weekend.
